title: Comparing Multiple Forecasters with SMCS
text: compare_forecasts() evaluates exactly two models, real-world applications often require comparing arbitrary number candidate models (m≥2m \ge 2) simultaneously. Evaluating multiple models sequentially introduces multiple-testing problem: run enough pairwise comparisons enough time steps, eventually find false “statistically significant” differences pure chance. solve , seqcomp implements Sequential Model Confidence Sets (SMCS) (Arnold et al., 2026). SMCS set models yet confidently beaten model candidate pool. package guarantees true best model(s) remain SMCS probability least 1−α1 - \alpha entire evaluation period. (comparing two forecasters, recommend starting introductory vignette.)

title: Comparing Multiple Forecasters with SMCS
text: comparing multiple models, seqcomp tracks two different definitions makes model “superior”: Strong Null (smcs_strong): model strongly superior performs least well every model every single time step. model consistently good occasional severe failures, eliminated set. Weak Null (smcs_weak): model weakly superior performs least well every model average time. allows models remain set even occasionally issue bad forecasts, provided long-term average remains dominant.

title: Comparing Multiple Forecasters with SMCS
text: Let’s generate sequence binary outcomes three candidate forecasters: M1: highly accurate forecaster. M2: mediocre forecaster guesses randomly. M3: terrible forecaster consistently wrong.
code: set.seed(2026) T_sim <- 300 y <- rbinom(T_sim, size = 1, prob = 0.7)  # Create 3 forecasters forecasts <- matrix(0, nrow = T_sim, ncol = 3) colnames(forecasts) <- c("M1", "M2", "M3")  forecasts[, "M1"] <- ifelse(y == 1, 0.8, 0.2)   # Highly accurate forecasts[, "M2"] <- runif(T_sim, 0.4, 0.6)     # Mediocre/random forecasts[, "M3"] <- ifelse(y == 1, 0.2, 0.8)   # Consistently wrong  head(forecasts) #>       M1        M2  M3 #> [1,] 0.8 0.5019408 0.2 #> [2,] 0.8 0.5009826 0.2 #> [3,] 0.8 0.5262100 0.2 #> [4,] 0.8 0.4685904 0.2 #> [5,] 0.8 0.5677538 0.2 #> [6,] 0.8 0.4215049 0.2

title: Comparing Multiple Forecasters with SMCS
text: smcs_strong() maintains running intersection time: model shown violate null competitor, excluded permanently. matches strong/uniformly-weak SMCS construction Arnold, Gavrilopoulos, Schulz Ziegel (2026, Section 3.2). underlying hypothesis smcs_weak() (time-varying weak null, Section 3.3) defined time tt, cumulatively, model’s average performance can legitimately recover bad stretch. smcs_weak() therefore returns smcs, can re-admit models previously excluded. Let’s look strong SMCS end evaluation: can visualize confidence set shrinks time plotting whether model TRUE (Included) FALSE (Excluded):  Notice quickly set shrinks: M3 (terrible model) confidently beaten M1 almost immediately drops set. M2 (mediocre model) survives bit longer, evidence accumulates, permanently excluded. M1 (true best model) remains SMCS entire duration.
code: tail(multi_cmp$smcs_strong) #>          M1    M2    M3 #> [295,] TRUE FALSE FALSE #> [296,] TRUE FALSE FALSE #> [297,] TRUE FALSE FALSE #> [298,] TRUE FALSE FALSE #> [299,] TRUE FALSE FALSE #> [300,] TRUE FALSE FALSE par(mfrow = c(3, 1), mar = c(2, 4, 2, 1)) colors <- c("blue", "gray", "red")  for (i in 1:3) {   plot(     1:T_sim, multi_cmp$smcs_strong[, i],      type = "s", col = colors[i], lwd = 2,     ylim = c(-0.1, 1.1), yaxt = "n", ylab = "In SMCS?",     main = paste("Model:", colnames(forecasts)[i])   )   axis(2, at = c(0, 1), labels = c("Excluded", "Included"), las = 2) } par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
